concepts.decision: Decide who may learn the information and under what conditions.
concepts.failureExample: A correctly delivered report is exposed to an unauthorized reader.
concepts.label: Confidentiality

concepts.decision: Test whether data remains accurate and complete through authorized changes.
concepts.definition: Protect against improper modification or destruction.
concepts.failureExample: A public transit arrival feed is altered while its service stays online.
concepts.label: Integrity

concepts.decision: Set the service deadline and tolerated interruption.
concepts.definition: Provide timely, reliable access for authorized use.
concepts.failureExample: An intact emergency roster cannot be retrieved during an evacuation.
concepts.label: Availability

concepts.decision: Validate identity or origin, including the trust binding.
concepts.definition: Establish that the claimed entity or information origin is genuine.
concepts.failureExample: An unmodified message comes from an impersonated sender.
concepts.label: Authenticity

concepts.decision: Bind the action to an identity and preserve evidence, context and integrity.
concepts.definition: Provide dependable evidence relevant to a later denial of an action.
concepts.failureExample: A mutable log with a shared account cannot reliably establish which person approved an action.
concepts.label: Nonrepudiation

concepts.decision: Select controls and tests against a specific protection outcome.
concepts.definition: State the asset, required property, consequence, accountable owner and measurable expectation.
concepts.failureExample: “Make the portal secure” gives neither a test nor a measurable acceptance criterion.
concepts.label: Security Requirements

misconceptions.claim: CIA is the entire security objective set.
misconceptions.correction: The outline also calls out authenticity and nonrepudiation; use the property that matches the decision.

outcome: Classify a business consequence by its relevant security property and select a proportionate protection objective.

sections.body: Confidentiality limits unauthorized disclosure. Integrity protects accuracy and completeness against unauthorized or improper change. Availability supports timely, reliable use. Authenticity provides confidence that an entity or information is genuine. Nonrepudiation strengthens evidence that a party performed an action. They often interact, but they are not interchangeable: encryption may support confidentiality, while a protected audit trail supports accountability and may contribute to nonrepudiation.
keyPoints: Start with the harmed property, not the technology.
One system can need different protection levels for each property.
sections.title: Five properties, different failures

sections.body: A useful requirement names the asset or service, the property, the failure consequence, and a measurable expectation. For example, an emergency dispatch service may prioritize availability and integrity, while a merger document may prioritize confidentiality and integrity. Requirements become inputs to risk analysis, architecture, testing, and continuity planning; vague phrases such as “make it secure” cannot be assessed or accepted.
keyPoints: Requirements make later control choices reviewable.
Authenticity answers whether a claimed source is genuine; nonrepudiation concerns durable action evidence.
sections.title: Turn properties into requirements

sections.body: Confidentiality limits unauthorized disclosure; integrity protects accuracy and completeness; availability preserves timely usable service; authenticity supports confidence in claimed identity or origin; and nonrepudiation relies on evidence and process sufficient to dispute denial of a meaningful act. For each property, name the asset, actor, state, consequence, control and measurable evidence. A confidentiality control can harm availability, and an integrity check does not prove origin; choose a balanced requirement rather than treating CIA or the five pillars as interchangeable slogans. Failure to distinguish the property produces the wrong test, control, and recovery objective.
keyPoints: Name the accountable owner, decision criterion, and evidence for each applicable outline topic.
Record the failure consequence and escalation or review trigger rather than assuming a policy label proves operation.

summary: Confidentiality, integrity, availability, authenticity, and nonrepudiation describe different protection outcomes. A sound decision identifies which outcome matters, to whom, and under what failure condition.
